newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mitterrand's allies pay tribute to EU statesman.
newsitem.headline: Mitterrand's allies pay tribute to EU statesman.

text.p: Francois Mitterrand's allies and sparring partners championed the late French president's European record on Thursday, denying on the first anniversary of his death that the fall of the Berlin Wall wrong-footed him.

Former foreign ministers Hans-Dietrich Genscher of Germany and David Owen of Britain, and ex-European Commission President Jacques Delors paid tribute to Mitterrand's 14-year rule at a two-day seminar hosted by UNESCO.

Genscher, among several "great witnesses" testifying on the legacy of socialist Mitterrand, heatedly rejected French reports of the time that the head of state did not see German reunification coming and that he was less than enthusiastic about it.
He quoted Mitterrand as telling him in Paris soon after the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 that German reunification was an "historical necessity and unavoidable".

"Mitterrand said that France stood on Germany's side but he asked which path Germany would follow -- would it be able to continue down the path of European union? (If not), the old alliances would have to be reconsidered.

"I owe it to him to say so: he was one of those who stood up for a reunified Germany and he wanted it to continue down the path of a united Europe," Genscher told an audience which included Mitterrand's widow Danielle and his former premiers Pierre Mauroy and Laurent Fabius.
Owen, appointed the European Union's mediator on former Yugoslavia in late 1992, hailed the late president as the European leader who worked the most to try and end the war.

"Mitterrand flew in to Sarajevo in June '92, that was a remarkably courageous personal intervention which opened up Sarajevo and allowed people to start doing something about the impending humanitarian disaster which was looming in the winter of '92," Owen said.

"After May 1993, we lost the chance of really stitching Bosnia-Herzegovina together but he was still engaged, still very committed on human rights. I look back to a man who was an immense help in that crisis," Owen added.

Delors and another former European Commission president, Gaston Thorn, credited Mitterrand with resolving in 1984 a long tussle with then prime minister Margaret Thatcher over Britain's contribution to the then European Community budget.
"When Thatcher agreed to a compromise, but made one last demand for an extra percentage point, Mitterrand agreed because he could see the long term," Delors said.
Earlier on Thursday, ex-leaders of several developing countries hailed Mitterrand's struggle for a fairer sharing of world resources and to lighten the foreign debt burden of the poorest countries.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Israeli ex-premier Shimon Peres and former United Nations chief Boutros Boutros-Ghali will address Friday's closing session.
But Cuban President Fidel Castro, who toured France in 1994 in a rare visit to the West, left a question mark hang over another visit. Organisers said he had not confirmed attendance.
Former U.S. and Soviet leaders George Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev declined the invitation because of prior commitments. Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak stayed away but sent a messge.
